finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. The only validation is that the string starts with https://, which does not block internal hosts (e.g. https://169.254.169.254/, https://users.internal:8080/, https://localhost/, private IPs, or internal hostnames). Axios follows redirects by default (up to 5), so an attacker-controlled HTTPS server can redirect to internal http:// targets. The response size is returned to the caller, giving a limited oracle for blind SSRF and internal port/host probing.
finding.source: req.body.avatarUrl (JSON body of POST /profile/avatar, attacker-controlled by any client)

trace.note: url = req.body.avatarUrl taken from request JSON
Only checks typeof string and startsWith('https://'); no host/IP allowlist, no private-range or DNS-resolution check, no redirect restriction
axios.get(url) performs the outbound request with default redirect following
Response body length is returned to the client (bytes), leaking reachability/size info

finding.guards_checked: Scheme check (https:// prefix) only. No hostname allowlist, no IP/private-range blocking, no DNS-rebinding protection, no maxRedirects:0, no authentication on the route. The https-only check limits plain-HTTP metadata endpoints directly but not HTTPS internal services or redirect-based bypass.

verdict.guard_found: Only a scheme-only check at server.js:11 (typeof string and startsWith("https://")); no host allowlist, no IP blocking, no redirect restriction, no auth middleware.
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl from an unauthenticated route, server.js:11 checks only the https:// prefix, and server.js:14 passes it to axios.get with default redirects, so the byte count returned at server.js:15 leaks internal reachability.

finding.claim: Dropped candidate, reported for completeness: GET /users/:id builds a URL from a fixed internal base and a path parameter. Path parameter is encodeURIComponent-encoded, so it cannot change host, scheme, or escape the path segment (no slashes). Only the path segment of a fixed host is controlled. Dot-segment values such as '..' are not encoded by encodeURIComponent and could traverse the path within the internal service (e.g. /v1/users/.. resolves to /v1/), but the host stays fixed. This is a low-impact path-manipulation issue, not true SSRF.

trace.note: URL composed with constant USER_SVC base; host fixed

finding.guards_checked: encodeURIComponent blocks '/', '?', '#', '@', ':' injection; host is hardcoded constant. Express decodes %2F in params, but re-encoding restores it. Only '.' and '..' remain unencoded.

verdict.guard_found: none closing for path traversal; only encodeURIComponent at server.js:19 (blocks / ? # @ : but not '.' or '..') and a constant host USER_SVC at server.js:7
verdict.reason: server.js:19-20 matches the trace, and req.params.id is attacker-controlled. encodeURIComponent leaves '..' unencoded, so `/users/..` reaches `/v1/` on the fixed host users.internal:8080. This is low-impact path manipulation within one internal service, not host-level SSRF, as the candidate itself says.
